extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and critics interested in race, colonial society, and religion (late-19th-century West Indies)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles the author uses to judge claims about race, labour, and religion in the colonial West Indies; the page offers standards for assessing historical, moral, religious, and sociological assertions. These criteria come from a literary/critical essay rebutting another author's alarmist conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical claim must be supported by law/usages
rubrics_metrics.description: "Never in the history of the British West Indies--must we again state--was there any law or usage establishing superiority in privileges for any section of the community on account of colour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author uses documentary/history standard: assertions of racial privilege require evidence of legal or customary enactment; absence of such evidence refutes claims of exclusive white domination. Example/usage: later demonstration that slave-owners were of all colours and that ownership, not skin, determined power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should be by salient qualities, not outward colour
rubrics_metrics.description: "classification in no department of science has ever been based on colour, but on relative affinity in certain salient qualities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy guidance: animals or pupils are grouped by essential traits (ability, affinity), not by colour. Use intellectual/functional criteria (competence, wealth, refinement) when dividing social classes rather than epidermal distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection for rule based on competence rather than skin
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is from the first mentioned that are selected those who are to bear the rule... There is no government by reason merely of skins."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political legitimacy and appointment should be assessed by merit/ability and circumstance rather than racial phenotype. Diversity of intelligence and circumstance explains leadership selection; do not attribute governance to 'skins' alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments must be morally reasonable and practically feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fatal objection to all Mr. Froude's advocacy of colour-domination is that it is futile from being morally unreasonable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond factual correctness, proposals must pass a test of moral sensibility and practical possibility: one cannot simply 'talk people into a frame of mind' incompatible with actual social conditions. Evaluate whether the mechanism proposed could realistically create the claimed social sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social esteem arises from concrete functions/wealth/valor, not colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Passage describing how hunters, mariners, and wealth-holders gained public admiration as societies changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use socio-historical causal criteria: esteem follows demonstrated utility (success in agriculture, bravery, commerce, wealth). Evaluate claims about social hierarchy by tracing practical sources of prestige in a given era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from biased or unrepresentative informants
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing a police official: his duties 'brought him in contact with the unfavourable specimens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing character of a group, beware witnesses whose role exposes them mainly to atypical or negative cases. Prefer representative sampling and context-aware testimony over anecdotal evidence from partial observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret observational anecdotes with attention to context
rubrics_metrics.description: Response to Froude's snapshot of garden-farm proprietors 'lounging about smoking' and women carrying market-baskets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-scale observations (market-day scenes, relaxed men) can be misleading if not contextualized (e.g., market routines, gendered division of labour). Avoid treating single vignettes as definitive evidence of character traits like indolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic outcomes (land ownership, emigration) as evidence of industriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the 'alarming absorption of the lands of Grenada and Trinidad by sable proprietors' and mass emigration to find work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use material indicators—land purchase, persistent emigration for labour, accumulation of money—to rebut claims of laziness. Correlate property ownership and migratory labour patterns with evidence of sustained work ethic and economic agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious creeds should be judged by practical moral conduct they produce
rubrics_metrics.description: "Religion... is purely a matter of feeling and action between man and man--the doing unto others as we would they should do unto us; and any creed... which directly or indirectly subverts or even weakens this basis is in itself a danger to the highest welfare of mankind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate religions by their observable social and moral consequences (charity, transformation, alleviation of Ignorance, Vice, Poverty) rather than abstract doctrinal coherence. The author lists historical exemplars (Paul, Vincent de Paul, Livingstone, etc.) as evidence of religion's positive outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: A creed imposed artificIally by outsiders is illegitimate and ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: "we protest against your right... to formulate for the special behoof of Negroes any sort of artificial creed unbelieved in by yourself..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance: religious or moral programs aimed at a people must be authentic, internally acceptable, and sincerely held; concocted or patronizing 'special' creeds lack moral authority and likely fail in practice. Anti-pattern: prescribing a faith one does not believe in for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance in refinement yields deeper moral sensibility, not mere loss of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: "with the advance of refinement, there is a concurrent growth in the intensity of moral sensibility, whereby the waning terrors of a future material hell are more than replaced by the agonies of a conscience self-convicted..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating secularizing trends, measure moral consciousness by internal conscience and responsibility rather than assuming loss of moral restraint. Claims that disbelief equates to moral laxity should be tested against evidence of heightened ethical sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the limits of scientific analysis regarding the Infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting rhetorical question: 'Canst thou by searching find out God; canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection!'; and critique of assuming telescopes/analysis can resolve questions of personal will or prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criterion: scientific tools (telescope, analysis) illuminate natural causes but do not by themselves conclusively negate religious belief; intellectual humility is required when discussing metaphysical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style/piquancy does not excuse factual or moral errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Author notes: 'piquancy is Mr. Froude's strong point, whatever else he may be found wanting in.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical skill or amusing phrasing (piquancy) should not be allowed to substitute for accurate evidence or morally sound argument. Critique style separately from substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The worth of religious/ethical claims is demonstrated by lives of beneficent exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Long list of historical exemplars (Paul, Augustine, Vincent de Paul, Francis Xavier, Matthew Hale, John Howard, Thomas Clarkson, Samuel Johnson, Henry Havelock, David Livingstone, Charles Gordon) used as evidence of Christianity's practical moral power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use biographical and historical examples of sustained beneficence, sacrifice, and transformation as evidence for the social efficacy of a creed. This is an evidentiary standard: doctrines gain credibility through demonstrated charitable action and human betterment.
